positions/lordship-salvation/oneLine: Saving faith includes repentance and submission to Jesus as Lord; though works do not earn salvation, a faith that produces no change is not saving faith.
positions/lordship-salvation/coreClaims/: Jesus’ gospel calls sinners to repent, deny themselves and follow him.
Faith is not mere assent but whole-hearted trust that includes surrender.
Genuine believers persevere and bear fruit; assurance involves the evidence of a changed life.
This is not salvation by works but salvation that works.
positions/lordship-salvation/origin: Named in the debate provoked by John MacArthur’s The Gospel According to Jesus (1988), defending the historic Reformed and Puritan view against the free grace position.
positions/lordship-salvation/strongestAr: It reflects the call of Jesus in the Gospels and the unity of justification and sanctification.
It warns nominal believers against false assurance.
It stands in continuity with Reformation teaching that faith alone justifies, but faith is never alone.
positions/lordship-salvation/strongestOb: Free grace: it makes assurance depend on works and adds conditions to the gospel.
Its demands can foster introspection and legalism.
Some Lutherans fear it blurs law and gospel.
positions/lordship-salvation/responses/0: Lordship advocates distinguish the ground of salvation (Christ alone) from its evidence (fruit).
positions/lordship-salvation/responses/1: They argue that assurance rests primarily on Christ’s promise, confirmed by the Spirit’s work.
positions/lordship-salvation/consequence: Shaped evangelical evangelism away from simple "decision" models in Reformed circles.
positions/new-perspective-on-paul/oneLin: Second Temple Judaism was a religion of grace, not legalism; Paul’s critique of "works of the law" targets Jewish boundary markers excluding Gentiles, and justification declares who belongs to God’s one covenant family.
positions/new-perspective-on-paul/coreCl: Judaism in Paul’s day was characterised by "covenantal nomism": election by grace, obedience as response (Sanders).
"Works of the law" refers especially to circumcision, food laws and Sabbath as ethnic badges (Dunn).
Justification is God’s covenant verdict that believers in Jesus — Jew and Gentile — belong to his people; future justification accords with the whole life (Wright).
Paul’s central themes include participation in Christ and the inclusion of the nations.
positions/new-perspective-on-paul/origin: Anticipated by Krister Stendahl (1963), launched by E. P. Sanders’ Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977), named by James Dunn (1982), popularised by N. T. Wright (What Saint Paul Really Said, 1997).
positions/new-perspective-on-paul/strong: It reads Paul within his Jewish setting and corrects caricatures of Judaism.
It explains why the Jew-Gentile question dominates Galatians and Romans.
It reconnects justification with ecclesiology and ethics.
Reformed and Lutheran critics (Piper, Westerholm, Carson): Paul also opposes human achievement (Rom 4:4-5) and imputation of righteousness is biblical.
Second Temple Judaism was more varied, and some texts show merit-based expectations ("variegated nomism").
It risks making justification by faith secondary and the final verdict dependent on works.
positions/new-perspective-on-paul/respon: Wright replies that he affirms the Reformers’ gospel but grounds it more fully in Paul’s covenant narrative.
Proponents note that many NPP insights (boundary markers, Gentile inclusion) are now widely accepted even by critics.
positions/new-perspective-on-paul/conseq: Reshaped Pauline scholarship since the 1980s and sparked the Piper-Wright debate (2007-09).
Encouraged Jewish-Christian rapprochement and ecumenical readings of justification.
positions/theosis/oneLine: Salvation is union with God: through the incarnate Son and the Holy Spirit, human beings become "partakers of the divine nature" and are transformed by grace into what God is by nature.
positions/theosis/coreClaims/0: God became human so that humans might become god by grace (Irenaeus, Athanasius).
positions/theosis/coreClaims/1: Salvation is healing from corruption and death and growth from image to likeness, not merely acquittal.
positions/theosis/coreClaims/2: Human freedom cooperates with grace (synergy) in prayer, sacraments and ascetic struggle.
positions/theosis/coreClaims/3: Deification never erases the distinction between Creator and creature.
positions/theosis/origin: Rooted in Irenaeus and Athanasius; term theosis coined by Gregory of Nazianzus; systematised by Pseudo-Dionysius and Maximus the Confessor (7th c.); central to Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and Church of the East piety.
positions/theosis/strongestArguments/0: It is rooted in the explicit language of Scripture and the consensus of the Greek fathers.
positions/theosis/strongestArguments/1: It unites incarnation, cross, resurrection, sacraments and holiness in one vision.
positions/theosis/strongestArguments/2: It avoids reducing salvation to legal status and affirms the goodness of human nature and the body.
positions/theosis/strongestObjections/0: Some Protestants: it risks blurring Creator and creature and downplays guilt, wrath and justification.
positions/theosis/strongestObjections/1: Its synergism can look semi-Pelagian to Augustinians.
positions/theosis/strongestObjections/2: Critics argue deification language owes more to Platonism than to Scripture.
positions/theosis/responses/0: Orthodox answer that deification is participation by grace in God’s energies, never in his essence, and presupposes forgiveness.
positions/theosis/responses/1: Western scholars have recovered deification themes in Augustine, Aquinas, Luther (Mannermaa) and Calvin (Billings), lessening the opposition.
positions/theosis/consequences/0: The governing vision of Eastern Christian spirituality, liturgy and monasticism.
positions/theosis/consequences/1: Increasingly drawn upon by Western theologians, including union-centred Protestants.
positions/palamite-essence-energies/oneL: God is unknowable and imparticipable in his essence, yet truly and wholly present and participable in his uncreated energies, so that the saints — as in the light of Tabor — experience God himself.
positions/palamite-essence-energies/core: God’s essence (ousia) remains beyond all knowledge and participation.
God’s energies (energeiai) are uncreated and are God himself in his self-communication.
The light of the Transfiguration seen by hesychasts in prayer is uncreated divine light.
Grace is not a created quality but God’s own life shared.
positions/palamite-essence-energies/orig: Gregory Palamas’ Triads (c.1338-1341) against Barlaam of Calabria; endorsed by councils at Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351; Palamas canonised 1368.
positions/palamite-essence-energies/stro: It preserves both divine transcendence and real communion with God.
It articulates the experience of hesychast saints and the Tabor tradition.
It makes theosis coherent: we become god by grace, not by essence.
Barlaam, Akindynos and later Western critics: it compromises divine simplicity by introducing a real distinction in God.
Some Catholics argued the uncreated light is either God’s essence or a created effect.
Critics question whether the distinction is found in the earlier fathers.
positions/palamite-essence-energies/resp: Palamites answer that the distinction is neither a division nor a composition in God, and is found in Basil and Maximus.
Recent Catholic and Protestant scholarship has become more sympathetic.
positions/palamite-essence-energies/cons: Dogmatic in Byzantine Orthodoxy after 1351; Sunday of St Gregory Palamas in Lent.
A point of East-West difference revisited in modern dialogue.
positions/origen-apokatastasis/oneLine: God’s goodness, working through Christ by persuasion and purifying punishment across ages, will restore all rational creatures to union with him, so that "the end is like the beginning" and God is all in all.
positions/origen-apokatastasis/coreClaim: All rational beings were created equal and free; their diversity results from their fall.
Punishment is medicinal and educational, not merely retributive.
Christ will subject all enemies to the Father by correcting them, so that God becomes all in all.
Origen sometimes speculated about the restoration even of the devil, though statements vary.
positions/origen-apokatastasis/origin: Origen of Alexandria, On First Principles (c.220-230) and later works; foreshadowed in Clement of Alexandria.
positions/origen-apokatastasis/strongest: It coheres with God’s universal will and with texts of all things reconciled.
It treats God’s punishments as just and remedial, like a physician’s.
It expresses confidence that evil, having no substance, cannot have the last word.
It depends on the pre-existence of souls and endless cycles of fall, which the church rejected.
If the devil can be saved and saints fall again, the stability of salvation is threatened.
It seems to contradict texts of eternal punishment (Matt 25:46).
positions/origen-apokatastasis/responses: Defenders note that aiōnios can mean "age-long" and that Origen held the restored will be confirmed in love.
Scholars such as Ramelli argue that many fathers shared restoration hopes without Origen’s cosmology.
positions/origen-apokatastasis/consequen: Condemned (in its Origenist form) by Justinian’s edict (543) and anathemas linked to Constantinople II (553).
Remained an underground current in East and West.
positions/gregory-of-nyssa-restoration/o: Because evil is non-being and God is infinite good, the fire of judgement purifies every soul until evil is wholly removed and all creation joins in thanksgiving to God.
positions/gregory-of-nyssa-restoration/c: Evil has no substance; it is a privation that cannot be eternal.
Judgement is a refining fire, painful in proportion to the evil to be removed.
In the end every knee will bow in genuine confession and God will be all in all.
Unlike Origen, Gregory does not teach pre-existence of souls or endless cycles.
positions/gregory-of-nyssa-restoration/o: Gregory of Nyssa (c.335-c.395), especially On the Soul and the Resurrection (with his sister Macrina, c.380), Catechetical Oration 26 and On the Life of Moses.
positions/gregory-of-nyssa-restoration/s: Gregory was honoured by the Second Council of Nicaea (787) as "father of fathers" and never condemned by name.
It grounds hope in the nature of God and of evil rather than speculative cosmology.
It echoes Pauline texts of God being all in all.
Most later fathers (Augustine, John Chrysostom, later Orthodox tradition) affirmed unending punishment.
Some argue Gregory’s statements were interpolated or misread.
It appears to neglect the seriousness of human freedom to persist in refusing God.
positions/gregory-of-nyssa-restoration/r: Many Orthodox today speak of a permitted "hope" for all (Balthasar’s "dare we hope", Kallistos Ware) rather than dogmatic certainty.
Scholars note Gregory’s restorationism is too pervasive to be a later interpolation.
positions/gregory-of-nyssa-restoration/c: Kept a tolerated hope of universal salvation alive within Orthodoxy.
positions/evangelical-universalism/oneLi: Salvation is only through Christ, by grace and faith, yet God’s love will in the end bring every person — after death if need be — to freely embrace Christ, so that hell is real but not endless.
positions/evangelical-universalism/coreC: Christ died for all and God desires and will accomplish the salvation of all.
Hell is a real, corrective punishment that can end in repentance.
Human freedom will not finally resist infinite love when its illusions are removed.
Distinct from pluralism: salvation is through Christ alone.
positions/evangelical-universalism/origi: Earlier forms: Elhanan Winchester’s The Universal Restoration (1788), the Universalist Church in America, George MacDonald; modern evangelical forms: Thomas Talbott (1999), Gregory MacDonald (Robin Parry, The Evangelical Universalist, 2006), David Bentley Hart (2019); debated popularly after Rob Bell’s Love Wins (2011).
positions/evangelical-universalism/stron: It takes the "all" texts at face value and gives God’s love final victory.
It solves moral objections to infinite punishment for finite sins.
It claims precedent in Gregory of Nyssa, Isaac of Nineveh and other fathers.
It contradicts the plain sense of Matthew 25:46, Revelation 14:11 and 20:10, and the church’s historic consensus.
It undercuts the urgency of evangelism and the seriousness of human choice.
Post-mortem conversion lacks clear scriptural basis.
positions/evangelical-universalism/respo: Universalists answer that "eternal" (aiōnios) qualifies the age to come rather than mere duration, and that the urgency of avoiding hell remains.
They argue God’s persuasion is compatible with freedom, as every conversion shows.
positions/evangelical-universalism/conse: A growing but contested minority among evangelicals and Orthodox.
Many denominations still treat it as outside their confessions.
